overview: This file contains two pieces of interdepartmental correspondence from November–December 1948 concerning U.S. efforts to alleviate a severe shortage of potassic fertilizer in occupied Japan, the Ryukyu Islands, and Korea. The Department of the Army describes requirements totaling 245,400 metric tons of contained K₂O, a reduced procurement target of approximately 151,600 tons, existing contracts and negotiations in Western and Soviet-occupied Europe, and bids for the remaining 56,700 tons. The Department of State approves additional purchases from Germany, including the Bizone and Soviet occupation zone, but withholds approval for further Spanish purchases because the Netherlands also depended on Spain to remedy a serious potash deficit and was already receiving special U.S. assistance with nitrogenous fertilizer.

subfiles.title: Army request for concurrence in Far Eastern potash procurement
subfiles.from: John P. Loomis, Deputy Food Administrator for Occupied Areas, Department of the Army
subfiles.to: Chief, International Resources Division, Department of State, attention C. W. Nichols
subfiles.about: The Army requests expedited State Department approval to purchase the balance of the minimum potash requirements for Japan, the Ryukyus, and Korea from Eastern Germany and possibly Spain.
subfiles.summary: Loomis reports that the occupied Far Eastern areas require 245,400 metric tons of contained K₂O, although the procurement program has been reduced to approximately 151,600 tons because of the worldwide fertilizer shortage. He inventories existing contracts and negotiations involving Spain, France, the Soviet occupation zone, the Netherlands, Bizonal Germany, and a Soviet trade representative in Tokyo, calculating that these arrangements would supply about 94,800 tons. To obtain the remaining 56,700 tons, the Army has received offers covering 35,300 tons from Spain and more than 150,000 tons from Eastern Germany. After noting ECA's lack of objection, he asks for rapid concurrence before the bidders' options expire.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on German and Spanish potash purchases
subfiles.from: C. W. Nichols, Assistant Chief, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.to: John P. Loomis, Deputy Food Administrator for Occupied Areas, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: The State Department approves additional procurement from Germany but declines to approve further purchases from Spain pending examination of their effect on Dutch and other European supplies.
subfiles.summary: Nichols acknowledges the Army's requirements and concurs in obtaining all or part of the additional 56,700 metric tons of K₂O from Germany, including the Bizone. He notes an understanding that the Army has sought first call on Bizonal exports for other occupied areas. The reply explains that the Netherlands had secured only 53 percent of its stated 1948–49 requirements and regarded Spain as its likeliest source of additional potash. Because further U.S. purchases could undermine Dutch fertilizer recovery and related American assistance, the Department declines for the time being to approve Spanish purchases beyond the 13,608 tons already under contract.

interest: The file supplies unusually precise figures for fertilizer requirements, contracts, bids, and countries of origin, making it valuable for reconstructing the material administration of the American occupation of East Asia. It also reveals the international allocation dilemmas created by postwar scarcity: agricultural recovery in Japan, Korea, and the Ryukyus competed directly with Dutch and wider European needs. Particularly striking is the willingness to procure large quantities from the Soviet occupation zone through a Soviet representative in Tokyo even as Marshall Plan agencies coordinated Western recovery, illustrating how practical supply needs could cut across emerging Cold War divisions.
